entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Chen Shou (233–297 CE) was the preeminent historian of the Three Kingdoms period, serving first the state of Shu Han and later the Western Jin dynasty. His monumental work, the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (*Sanguozhi*), stands as the foundational official history of this tumultuous era (220–280 CE), providing critical biographical and chronological accounts of the rival states of Wei, Shu, and Wu. Born in Baxi Commandery (modern Sichuan), Chen Shou’s unique position allowed him to compile firsthand accounts and existing records from the perspective of a participant, solidifying his legacy as a pivotal figure in Chinese historiography.

After serving as a scribe and official in Shu Han, Chen Shou’s career was interrupted by the conquest of Shu by Wei in 263 CE. He later found employment under the unified Western Jin dynasty, which sought to legitimate its rule by sponsoring the compilation of a comprehensive history of the preceding period. Drawing upon a wealth of primary sources, including official documents, private writings, and oral traditions, Chen Shou meticulously crafted the *Sanguozhi* into 65 volumes. His methodology, though sometimes criticized for brevity or selective inclusion, was groundbreaking for its time, focusing on biographical narratives and incorporating a critical perspective on his sources, even as he faced political pressures and personal biases.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Chen Shou's *Records of the Three Kingdoms* established the canonical historical narrative for a pivotal period in Chinese history, influencing not only subsequent scholarship but also the cultural memory of East Asia through its impact on popular literature. His work remains the primary source for understanding the Three Kingdoms period.
